الفاو تحذر.. موجة غلاء عالمية جديدة على الأبواب. يدق العالم طبول أزمة غذاء جديدة، إذ تتضافر الحروب وارتفاع أسعار الطاقة وتغير المناخ لدفع الأسعار نحو ارتفاعات قياسية، وفي السودان تسجل الأسواق قفزات متسارعة، وسط تحذيرات أممية متصاعدة.

كم تبلغ تكلفة إعادة بناء غزة؟ ومن أين سيأتي التمويل؟. تواجه غزة بعد توقف القتال معركة شاقة لإعادة الإعمار، حيث تُقدر التكلفة الإجمالية بنحو 71 مليار دولار وفقا لتقارير دولية، في حين لم تتجاوز التعهدات العالمية 17 مليار دولار، مما يترك فجوة تمويلية هائلة.

مصادر عبرية: تضاعف معدل الهجرة من إسرائيل وخسائر بمئات الملايين. قالت صحيفة "إسرائيل هيوم" إن وثيقة داخلية لسلطة الضرائب الإسرائيلية أظهرت أن تسارع هجرة الإسرائيليين الأثرياء يحرم الخزينة من إيرادات ضريبية تُقدّر بمتوسط 700 مليون شيكل (232 مليون دولار) سنويا.
دراسة تتوقع العمر الذي يصبح فيه مبابي مليارديرا. بعد كريستيانو رونالدو وليونيل ميسي، تتوقع دراسة أن ينضم كيليان مبابي إلى نادي الرياضيين المليارديرات، لكنْ لا يزال الطريق أمامه طويلا.

إيران مباشر.. ترمب يتحدث عن نهاية وشيكة للحرب وسط استياء بشأن نقص الذخيرة. نقلت صحيفة وول ستريت جورنال عن مسؤولين قولهم إن ترمب طلب إجراء تحقيقات بشأن تسريبات نقص مخزون الذخيرة، في حين ذكرت مصادر إيرانية لوكالة تسنيم سماع دويّ انفجارين في جزيرة قشم إثر التصدي لأهداف معادية.

لماذا تعاقد ريال مدريد مع ديوماندي وكيف سينسجم مع خط الهجوم المليء بالنجوم؟. لماذا أنفق ريال مدريد مبالغ طائلة لضم نجم كأس العالم إلى خط هجوم يضم بالفعل كيليان مبابي، وجود بيلينغهام، وفينيسيوس جونيور؟

السعودية تتوقع هجمات منسقة من الفصائل العراقية والحوثيين. قال ⁠مسؤول ⁠سعودي إن تقارير مخابراتية -من المملكة ⁠والولايات المتحدة ​ودول بالشرق الأوسط- ⁠تشير إلى تنسيق فصائل ​مسلحة عراقية مع جماعة الحوثيون اليمنية، من ‌أجل شن هجمات ​وشيكة على السعودية.

بالفيديو.. موقف محرج لهداف الدوري الكولومبي أثناء تكريمه. وجد مهاجم كولومبي نفسه في موقف غير متوقع قبل مباراة بالدوري المحلي، بعدما تحول حفل تكريمه إلى لقطة لافتة أثارت تفاعلا واسعا على مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي.
برشلونة يلغي مباراة ودية في طنجة بسبب أزمة سبتة. يعتقد نادي برشلونة أن الظروف الراهنة غير مواتية لإقامة مباراته الودية التي كانت مقررة في طنجة يوم 15 أغسطس/آب الجاري.

أريانا غراندي وبريتني سبيرز وجاستن بيبر في مواجهة وحش الشهرة. يعيد قرار أريانا غراندي الابتعاد عن الأضواء فتح ملف الثمن النفسي للشهرة، عبر استعراض قصص نجوم دفعتهم الضغوط الإعلامية وثقافة المراقبة المستمرة إلى الانسحاب المؤقت أو إعادة رسم علاقتهم بالنجومية.

من يخلف دانيال كريغ؟ العد التنازلي للكشف عن جيمس بوند الجديد. بعد سنوات من الانتظار، يبدو أن الغموض يقترب أخيرا من نهايته، مع توقعات بالكشف عن هوية البطل الجديد قبل نهاية عام 2026، إيذانا ببدء حقبة جديدة لإحدى أشهر الشخصيات في تاريخ السينما.

بعد صدمة سبتة.. ما أكبر تحدٍّ يواجه أوروبا في ملف الهجرة؟. انقشعت أزمة تدفق عشرات الآلاف من المهاجرين عبر الحدود الفاصلة مع المغرب نحو مدينة سبتة، بيد أن التداعيات والارتدادات السياسية أحدثت تصدعات عميقة في القارة العجوز.

إصابات لا تُرى.. حرب إيران تعيد فتح ملف أدمغة الجنود الأمريكيين. أعادت حرب إيران فتح ملف إصابات الدماغ لدى الجنود الأمريكيين، بعد إصابة نحو 700 عسكري وعودة معظمهم إلى الخدمة، وسط تحذيرات من آثار قد تستمر لسنوات.

زامير يعلن ملاحقة نخبة حماس.. فما مصير خريطة مجلس السلام؟. في تصريحات أكدت تمسك إسرائيل باستمرار العمليات العسكرية، أكد رئيس أركان الجيش إيال زامير عزم قواته على مواصلة استهداف عناصر "النخبة" في حركة المقاومة الإسلامية (حماس).
الاتحاد الإنجليزي يسحب دعمه لإنفانتينو. انضم الاتحاد الإنجليزي لكرة القدم رسميا إلى جبهة المعارضة الدولية ضد رئيس الاتحاد الدولي (فيفا) جياني إنفانتينو.

ما وراء الخبر.. حماس تقبل بحصر السلاح مقابل الانسحاب وإسرائيل تتمسك بالانتقام. كشف رئيس أركان الجيش الإسرائيلي إيال زامير خطة لاستمرار ملاحقة عناصر نخبة حركة المقاومة الإسلامية (حماس)، رغم تقارير عن تقييد الاغتيالات استجابة لخريطة مجلس السلام.

إسلام آباد من الخليج إلى باب المندب.. باكستان في قلب البنية الأمنية الخليجية. في وقت تتصاعد فيه التهديدات على الملاحة في البحر الأحمر وباب المندب، وتترنح المظلة الأمنية الأمريكية بين الالتزام والتقلب، تعيد السعودية رسم خريطتها الأمنية من خلال تحالفات جديدة، وقدرات ردع مركبة.

مصادر: السعودية وباكستان وتركيا ستوقّع اتفاقية دفاع مشترك اليوم. قالت مصادر سعودية إن ولي العهد السعودي الأمير محمد بن سلمان والرئيس التركي رجب طيب أردوغان ورئيس الوزراء الباكستاني شهباز شريف سيوقّعون اتفاقية دفاع مشترك اليوم الجمعة في مدينة جدّة.

أثارت غضب ترمب.. ماذا تُخفي تقارير مخزون الأسلحة الأمريكية؟. أثارت تقارير استخباراتية عن تراجع مخزون الأسلحة الأمريكية استياء الرئيس الأمريكي دونالد ترمب، خشية تأثيرها على صورة واشنطن وموقعها في وقت حساس من الصراع الجاري مع إيران.

أوروبا في مواجهة أزمات تهدد مستقبلها. تكشف تقارير صحفية عن حجم الضغوط التي تواجهها أوروبا، وعن صعوبة تحولها إلى قوة مستقلة قادرة على التحكم في مسارات الأحداث، بدلاً من الاكتفاء بالتعامل مع أزمات تصنعها في كثير من الأحيان قوى خارج حدودها.

لماذا رفضت إسرائيل اتفاق غزة بينما قبلته حماس؟. رأت مجلة "فورين بوليسي" أن نزع سلاح حركة حماس ظل -منذ أشهر- العقبة الرئيسية أمام إحراز تقدم في عملية السلام المتعثرة، ولكن سرعان ما اتضح -بعد موافقتها- أن الموقف الإسرائيلي لا يتطابق مع هذا التقييم.

غارديان: أزمة سبتة تختبر رهان سانشيز على إسبانيا المستقلة. أثار وصول آلاف المهاجرين إلى سبتة موجة واسعة من الجدل داخل الأوساط اليمينية المتطرفة في أوروبا، كما دفع عددا من القادة الأوروبيين إلى توجيه انتقادات مباشرة لسياسة رئيس الوزراء الإسباني في ملف الهجرة.

الاحتلال ينسحب من قلنديا بعد اقتحام خلّف دمارا واعتقالات بالعشرات. خلّفت اعتداءات جيش الاحتلال الإسرائيلي والمستوطنين في الضفة الغربية المحتلة إصابات ودمارا، بعد اقتحام لمخيم قلنديا شمال القدس المحتلة، وهجوم استهدف تجمع خربة الطوبا جنوب الضفة الغربية.

الادعاء الإسرائيلي يكتفي بتوجيه تهمة القتل الخطأ لقاتل عودة الهذالين. وجّه الادعاء العام الإسرائيلي تهمة القتل غير العمد إلى مستوطن في قضية مقتل الناشط الفلسطيني عودة الهذالين، رغم إطلاق النار عليه مباشرة.

الحوثيون يهاجمون معسكرات حكومية ويقصفون نجران بالسعودية. دخل التصعيد بين الحوثيين والسعودية مرحلة جديدة بعد هجمات استهدفت القوات الحكومية اليمنية وأعقبتها ضربات عبر الحدود، وسط مخاوف من اتساع رقعة الصراع.

Why Israel's opposition no longer wants Palestinian parties in government Submitted by Samah Watad on Thu, 08/06/2026 - 14:31 Anti-Netanyahu leaders who once defended cooperation with Palestinian parties now rule it out, reflecting a broader post-7 October shift in Israeli politics Arab Israeli lawmakers Mansour Abbas (L) and Ayman Odeh (R) at the Knesset in Jerusalem on 29 December 2022 (Amir Cohen/AFP) Off Gadi Eisenkot last week became the latest Israeli politician to pledge to form a "Zionist majority" government if he became Israel's next prime minister. The phrase is widely understood as ruling out a coalition with Palestinian Arab parties to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "I prefer to achieve a Zionist majority of 63-64 seats, and if that doesn't happen, to call on the ultra-Orthodox parties to understand the gravity of the moment," Eisenkot, a former general and leader of the Yashar party, said at a security conference organised by Yedioth Ahronoth and the Institute for National Security Studies. "If they don't understand, then it's better to go to new elections," he added. His remarks reflect a broader shift. From Naftali Bennett to Yair Lapid, leaders across the anti-Netanyahu camp have increasingly ruled out forming a government that relies on Palestinian Arab parties, including the United Arab List (Ra'am), whose leader, Mansour Abbas, has repeatedly said he is willing to negotiate with Jewish-majority parties. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The change is striking. Bennett and Lapid defended their partnership with Abbas in the 2021 coalition as a necessary political experiment that ended Netanyahu's 12-year hold on power. Today, the post-7 October reality in Israel has made such cooperation politically costly. Who is Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief challenging Netanyahu? Read More » "This is first and foremost the result of the shift in Israeli public opinion after 7 October," Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst, told Middle East Eye. "Any partnership with a Palestinian Arab party is now presented electorally as a concession on security and identity. Even parties in the political centre fear being portrayed as relying on those who reject the Jewish character of the state." The election, scheduled for 27 October, is widely seen as pivotal for Israel's political future. Polls show an Eisenkot-led bloc running neck and neck with Netanyahu's. Some surveys suggest Eisenkot could win enough seats to govern without Palestinian Arab parties, while others indicate that neither bloc is likely to secure a parliamentary majority without their backing. Taboo returns Palestinian parties represent Palestinian citizens of Israel , the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homeland after Zionist militias displaced around 750,000 people in 1948 to create the state of Israel, an event Palestinians refer to as the Nakba . Today, the community numbers about two million people, accounting for roughly a fifth of Israel's population. After decades of discrimination, Palestinian citizens of Israel established political parties to advocate civil equality, an end to the occupation and recognition of Palestinian national rights. For decades, however, those parties remained on the margins of Israeli politics. Cooperation with governing coalitions was widely viewed as politically toxic by much of the Jewish electorate and many Palestinian citizens alike. That taboo was broken in 2021, when Ra'am became kingmaker, providing the four seats needed for Bennett and Lapid to assemble a razor-thin majority and end Netanyahu's rule after four inconclusive elections. 'Today, the political cost of being seen as close to Palestinian Arab parties has become very high' – Ehab Jabareen, political analyst Since the Hamas-led attacks of October 2023, however, the taboo has largely returned. According to the Israel Democracy Institute's Democracy Index, published in December 2025, 71.5 percent of Jewish Israelis opposed including Arab parties in the next government. A separate 2025 survey by the Institute for National Security Studies found that 57 percent of Israelis opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state under any circumstances, underscoring the hardening of public opinion. "Netanyahu succeeded in turning relations with Palestinian Arab parties into an electoral weapon," Jabareen said, referring to years of campaigning that portrayed cooperation with Palestinian politicians as politically illegitimate. "Today, the political cost of being seen as close to Palestinian Arab parties has become very high." Jabareen believes some parties could still seek the support of Palestinian Arab parties after the election if the parliamentary arithmetic leaves them with no alternative. During the campaign, however, few are willing to signal that possibility. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "They keep the back door open, but the front door is locked." Politics of the possible The increasingly hostile political climate towards Palestinian citizens of Israel since October 2023 has also reshaped the strategy of Palestinian parties. For years, Abbas has maintained that Ra'am is willing to negotiate with any coalition capable of replacing Netanyahu, despite repeated declarations from opposition leaders ruling out such cooperation. Mansour Abbas: An icon for supporters of Israeli settler-colonialism Read More » This election cycle, however, he has gone further. Israeli media have reported that Ra'am has reached an agreement in principle with Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former Yesh Atid lawmaker, to include him on the party's electoral list. A Channel 13 poll suggested Segalovich's inclusion could lift Ra'am's projected representation from five seats to an unprecedented seven. Jabareen says Abbas is speaking to three audiences at once: Palestinian voters, the anti-Netanyahu camp and the Israeli establishment. "He wants to tell Palestinian Arab voters that he is still the only one practising the politics of the possible," says Jabareen. "At the same time, he is leaving the anti-Netanyahu camp an exit if it eventually needs the support of non-Zionist parties, while signalling to the Israeli establishment that Ra'am remains a reliable institutional partner." But the strategy also carries risks. "He is signalling a willingness to negotiate with a side that publicly says it has no interest in negotiating with him," Jabareen said. "That creates an image of weakness because the balance of power is not in his favour." Should Palestinians run for the Knesset? For Aida Touma-Sliman, a Knesset member from Hadash, a Palestinian-led party, the refusal of Jewish parties to work with Palestinian parties reflects more than electoral strategy. "The leaders of these parties know the Israeli public does not want any partnership with Palestinian Arab parties after years of incitement," she told MEE. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "They lack the courage to present a genuine alternative to the current government's policies. In reality, they also hold Zionist and discriminatory positions." Ahead of Israel's elections, Bennett rejects two-state solution as Eisenkot surges in polls Read More » Touma-Sliman also rejects the idea that joining a governing coalition should be the primary objective of Palestinian parties. "Our presence in the Knesset was never based solely on joining governments," she said. "It is a space for political struggle where we represent our community, expose government policies and defend our people's rights." While she acknowledges that parliament is no longer the only arena for political action, she argues that abandoning it would only weaken Palestinian citizens' influence at a time when, she says, "our political weight is needed to confront fascism, even if that only means preventing the formation of another far-right government". For Jabareen, however, the challenge extends beyond coalition politics. He argues that Palestinian parties have spent too many election campaigns focused on which government they might help form, even as Israel's political landscape has fundamentally changed. "The important question is no longer who will invite us into a coalition," he said. "The real question is how we rebuild Palestinian political power inside Israel over the next decade in a way that makes ignoring us politically costly." FO slams India's remarks on AJK polls, says it has no 'standing or moral authority' to comment on process. The Foreign Office (FO) said on Thursday that India had “neither the standing nor the moral authority” to comment on the elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), which are being held in phases amid security concerns and unrest in the region. FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi made the remarks while addressing a weekly press briefing, where he was asked about the Indian External Affairs Ministry’s (MEA) “reaction” to the ongoing polls. While the question did not elaborate further, the Indian ministry had termed the polls a “farce” on Tuesday, saying that such “hollow exercises” could not hide the reality. “Pakistan categorically rejects the baseless and politically motivated remarks of the Indian MEA regarding the ongoing legislative elections in the AJK,” Andrabi said on Thursday. “It is unsurprising that India has chosen to issue such remarks on the eve of the 7th anniversary of its illegal and unilateral actions of August 5 , through which it seeks to alter the internationally recognised disputed status of Jammu and Kashmir,” he said, adding that actions violated the relevant UN Security Council (UNSC) resolutions, international law, and India’s international commitments. Andrabi held that elections in AJK were being conducted in a “peaceful, transparent and orderly manner” in accordance with the constitutional and legal framework governing the region. He added that the ongoing elections reflected “democratic aspirations and political will of the people of AJK”. Andrabi maintained that India, in view of its continued denial of fundamental political rights and democratic freedom in occupied Kashmir, “has neither the standing nor the moral authority to comment on the democratic process in AJK”. He added that misinformation and propaganda could not change the status of occupied Kashmir, which remained a disputed territory. “Its final disposition is to be determined in accordance with relevant UNSC resolutions as well as the freely expressed will of the Kashmiri people and through a UN-administered plebiscite,” he said. He also held that India’s “attempt to invoke misleading casualty figures” cannot obscure its own actions in occupied Kashmir. Andrabi said such statements were an attempt to deflect international attention away from India’s “continued violation of international human rights and humanitarian law and its persistent failure to fulfil international obligations”. At this, he called on the neighbouring India to reverse its illegal actions of August 5, 2019 and “create an environment conducive to peaceful settlement in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions”. The FO spokesperson was also asked about the Indian ministry’s response to comments made by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on the occasion of Youm-i-Istehsal wherein it had condemned Pakistan’s “desperate peddling of falsehoods”. He held that the Indian MEA statement was a “self-serving eulogy” for its actions in the occupied Kashmir. “The reality is that a prolonged and heavy military presence, coupled with draconian laws, continues to facilitate demographic change aimed at altering the territory’s Muslim majority character.” The FO spokesperson also took note of India’s “systemic efforts” suppressing the voices of Kashmiri people and that its “so-called development” in the occupied territory was not a substitute for the rights of the Kashmiri people. “We remain unwavering in our support for the just [..] and call upon India to reverse its illegal and unilateral measures and its human rights violations and engage in the peaceful resolution of Jammu and Kashmir.” Pakistan continues engagement on US-Iran Speaking about Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to mediate between the US and Iran, the FO spokesperson said that Pakistan remained engaged to resolve the crisis, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz. He vowed that Pakistan would continue to “actively pursue diplomatic engagements and support all sincere efforts aimed at achieving a comprehensive, just and lasting resolution to the conflict”. Andrabi also hoped that an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz would lead to the resumption of talks between the US and Iran under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) , AFP reported. “We hope that the agreement on the Strait will pave the way for continuing dialogue, particularly the resumption of technical-level talks between Iran and the US,” the foreign ministry spokesman told reporters. Andrabi also lauded Oman for its “valuable and steadfast” efforts towards de-escalation, particularly as a littoral state to the State of Hormuz.

IHC reserves order on pleas against Imran, Bushra’s alleged solitary confinement. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday reserved its order on petitions seeking to declare the alleged solitary confinement of PTI founder Imran Khan and his spouse Bushra Bibi illegal after hearing detailed arguments from both sides. Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro observed that the court would issue an order after examining the record and directed the parties to submit in writing any judgments they wished to rely on. During the hearing, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Islamabad Advocate General Naveed Hayat Malik and counsel for the petitioners Barrister Salman Safdar appeared before the court. The advocate general argued that the petitions were not maintainable and maintained that neither Imran nor Bushra had been kept in solitary confinement. He said the prison authorities had instead provided them with facilities exceeding those available to B-class prisoners. He submitted that, owing to security considerations arising from Imran’s political profile, he had been housed separately from other inmates, but such arrangements could not be termed solitary confinement. The jail authorities, he added, had complied with previous court directions by providing newspapers, books and other facilities. Justice Soomro questioned the nature of the security arrangements and asked whether Imran had been extended B-class facilities. The advocate general replied that he was receiving facilities even better than those prescribed for B-class prisoners. Superintendent Sajid Baig informed the court that Imran had been provided more than 500 books so far, besides daily newspapers. He said the PTI founder was not confined to a single cell for 24 hours, explaining that he had access to a compound comprising seven cells where he could move freely during the day. He further contended that the concept of solitary confinement required a prisoner to remain locked in a cell continuously, which was not the case. The advocate general further argued that neither any court nor any competent authority had ordered solitary confinement for either Imran Khan or Bushra Bibi, and that the petitioners could not seek relief beyond what was prayed for in their petitions. Barrister Salman Safdar disputed the government’s stance, arguing that his clients were effectively being subjected to prolonged isolation amounting to mental torture. Referring to his meeting with Imran earlier this year on the Supreme Court’s directions, he said his client had complained of deteriorating eyesight, restricted access to lawyers, political colleagues and family members, and an inadequate supply of books. He told the court that despite facing more than 300 criminal cases, Imran had not been allowed regular consultations with his legal team. According to the counsel, a 65-minute meeting arranged in April following the intervention of the IHC chief justice was the first meaningful consultation after several months, during which most of the discussion centred on the alleged mental distress caused by prison conditions. Justice Soomro asked whether the petitioner had supported the allegations through an affidavit. Barrister Safdar replied that he intended to address every aspect of the case through his arguments. The counsel requested the court to appoint a panel of lawyers to inspect prison conditions, allow weekly telephone conversations between Imran Khan and his two sons, facilitate regular meetings with lawyers and family members, and direct the authorities to permit Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi to spend time together in accordance with prison rules. During the proceedings, books sent by Imran’s family for delivery to the prison were produced before the court, prompting Justice Soomro to seek the list of the books. Aleema Khan also addressed the court, alleging that her brother had received only three books since December and had met family members only a handful of times, mostly pursuant to court orders. She urged the court to direct the prison authorities to produce a complete record of meetings. The advocate general objected to the issue of Imran’s eyesight being raised in the present proceedings, arguing that it was outside the scope of the petitions. Justice Soomro, however, remarked that it would have been appropriate had the medical board’s report also been placed before the court. Separately, the Adiala jail superintendent submitted a report denying that Bushra Bibi had been kept in solitary confinement or subjected to discriminatory treatment. The report stated that the practice of solitary confinement had virtually ceased in prisons and that Bushra Bibi was being accommodated separately only because of security concerns arising from her status as the spouse of a former prime minister. It said she had access to a spacious room, a separate courtyard and kitchen, could move freely within the designated area during the day, received regular medical examinations by female prison staff and was allowed to meet Imran Khan every Tuesday in accordance with prison rules. After completion of arguments, Justice Soomro reserved the matter, observing that any judicial precedents relied upon by the parties should be submitted in writing before the court passed its order. PTI ‘strongly rejects’ report Meanwhile, the PTI “strongly rejected” the report submitted by Adiala jail authorities before the IHC. “The reality is that Imran Khan has been subjected to extremely strict and extraordinary restrictions for a prolonged period. Regular meetings with his sisters and other family members have consistently been obstructed, and his right to visitation has repeatedly been restricted despite court orders. “Likewise, Imran Khan has not been allowed access to his personal physician for medical examination and treatment, raising serious concerns about his health,” the party said in a statement. The PTI further demanded the “immediate and full implementation” of all court orders, the provision of Imran’s constitutional and legal rights without discrimination, unrestricted meetings with his family members and lawyers, and an immediate medical examination by his personal physician.

Over 1,900 cases of child abuse reported in first half of the year: report. ISLAMABAD: In the first six months of the year, 1,914 cases of child abuse were reported across the country, child protection NGO Sahil said in its latest report. Among the reported cases, 49 involved infants who were found abandoned by the roadside. From January to June 2026, as many as 1,015 cases of child sexual abuse, 558 cases of abduction, 101 cases of missing children and 35 cases of child marriages were reported. Furthermore, 98 cases of pornography following sexual abuse were also recorded. The Sahil report was compiled on the basis of data collected from different national and regional newspapers of all four provinces, including Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and Gilgit-Baltistan (GB). Of the total reported cases, 58 per cent of victims were girls. The data also showed that children aged 11-15 years were the most vulnerable to abuse. Among the victims, 598 children were aged between 11 and 15, 356 were aged 16-18, 329 belonged to the 6-10 years age bracket, while 95 victims were between zero and five years old. In 487 cases, the ages of the victims were not mentioned. The report also sheds light on the risks children can face in the presence of known people. The abusers involved in 43pc of the reported cases were acquaintances, while in 34pc of cases, the perpetrators were identified as strangers. Almost half of the reported incidents of abuse — 45pc — took place at the victims’ own residences, while 18pc occurred at the abusers’ houses. A smaller proportion, 3pc, took place in open fields, while in 21pc of cases, the place of abuse was not specified. More cases were reported in urban areas than in rural areas, with the split standing at 57pc and 43pc, respectively. An overwhelming majority — 80pc — of the cases took place in the most-populated province of Punjab , followed by Sindh where 15pc of the reported cases took place. The rest of the country made up the remaining 5pc of the reported cases. According to the data, 89pc cases were registered with the police, while the status of case registration was not mentioned for the rest of the cases. The report reveals that seven cases were “unregistered with police” and in one case, police refused to register the case.

PM Shehbaz arrives in Saudi Arabia on 3-day visit. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, accompanied by the Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in Saudi Arabia on Thursday evening for a three-day visit. Apart from CDF Munir, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar and Special Assistant Tariq Fatemi are also accompanying the premier on the visit. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar, who is currently in Saudi Arabia after concluding a visit to Jordan, will be part of the delegation as well. In a post on X, the government said the premier landed in Jeddah and was received by Deputy Governor of Makkah Prince Saud bin Mishal bin Abdulaziz at the airport. Saudi Minister of Agriculture, Water, and Environment Engineer Abdulrahman and Pakistan’s Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Ahmad Farooq were also among the officials present to greet PM Shehbaz. The premier will also perform Umrah and visit Holy Prophet’s (PBUH) mosque in Madina during the visit, the government said. Earlier, FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi announced the visit in a weekly briefing. “During the visit, the prime minister will meet the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and discussions will focus on consolidating the Pakistan-Saudi bilateral relationship and exchange views on areas of regional and international developments of mutual interests,” he said. He stressed that the visit marked Pakistan’s “long-standing partnership” with Saudi Arabia, which he said was “anchored in decades of mutual trust, cooperation and brotherhood”. Andrabi noted that while the visit was taking place amid heightened tensions in the Gulf, he said that “it will carry immense significance beyond the immediate crisis and short-term considerations”. He added that the visit will “further strengthen bilateral relations, deepen strategic cooperation, enhance coordination on regional and international issues of mutual interest and also reinforce multilateral cooperation”. Shortly after, an official statement regarding the visit was also issued. The premier had last visited Saudi Arabia in April, meeting with the kingdom’s top leadership. As the Middle East conflict has expanded across new fronts, Saudi Arabia has unveiled plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition to protect shipping and energy supply routes in the Red Sea region. Fourteen countries, including Pakistan, have voiced support for the coalition. In July, Pakistan also endorsed Saudi Arabia’s air strikes in Iraq as an exercise of its right to self-defence. The remarks came two days after Saudi Arabia and the US carried out coordinated strikes against installations of Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Units, accusing elements within the umbrella force of launching attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The remarks followed Pakistan’s earlier warning after Yemen’s Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade targeting shipping linked to Saudi Arabia. Islamabad had then described attacks on Pakistani maritime interests as a “red line”, warning that any hostile action against Pakistani-flagged vessels or commercial shipping would be treated as an attack on Pakistan. The country also simultaneously reaffirmed its commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security and the uninterrupted flow of lawful maritime commerce through the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb. Last year, Islamabad and Riyadh concluded a Strategic Mutual Defence Agree­ment, which became operational earlier this year as Pakistan simultaneously embarked on a diplomatic effort to mediate between Iran and the United States.

Spent cartridge casing recovered from crime scene in Mir Raza Ali case: police. KARACHI: Police on Thursday claimed to have made a major breakthrough in the case of Mir Raza Ali after recovering a spent cartridge casing from the crime scene in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. Raza, an IBA graduate and owner of the eatery Wafflix, went missing on July 28. The 25-year-old’s body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. Special Investigation Unit (SIU) Senior Superintendent of Police Dr Samiullah Soomro, who heads the probe team, told Dawn that the police recovered “a fired bullet shell from the crime scene during a meticulously planned search operation”. He added that a special search team, comprising four station house officers (SHOs) and 40 constables, was formed to conduct a comprehensive examination of the crime scene. Equipped with metal detectors and other equipment, the team divided the area into four sectors, with each unit assigned a separate search pattern and sector to ensure complete coverage of the scene. “The painstaking search resulted in the recovery of a fired bullet shell from a location consistent with the projected bullet trajectory in relation to the position of the deceased,” said the officer, terming it a “major breakthrough”. Investigators described the recovery as a critical piece of physical evidence and expected it to play a “pivotal role” in forensic examination, ballistic analysis and reconstruction of the sequence of events surrounding the incident. Earlier today, a Karachi court issued an order to exhume Ali’s remains for further investigation. The court issued the order on an application filed by Ali’s father, after a controversy emerged between the Karachi police surgeon and investigators over alleged loopholes in the medico-legal report regarding the post-mortem examination. In its order, the court directed the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medico-legal board for the exhumation of Ali’s body “under intimation to this court at the earliest possible date and time”. The court order, issued after the ruling by Judicial Magistrate Hameedullah, stated that Ali’s father, Mir Hussain Ali Khan, had filed an application seeking the exhumation of his son’s body in accordance with law. He also requested the formation of a medico-legal board, comprising senior forensic experts and pathologists, under the Karachi police surgeon “to conduct a fresh and comprehensive” medico-legal examination and postmortem, as well as X-ray, DNA, forensic and chemical examination of the body to ascertain the actual cause of death. The case took a turn when Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed told a private news channel on Tuesday that the postmortem findings of Ali’s body had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. She said the reported entry wound, bullet trajectory and exit wound did not correspond with one another. While it was scientifically possible for a bullet to enter through the back and exit from the front, she stressed that her assessment was based only on the postmortem report and photographs, as she had not examined the body herself. The police surgeon noted that entry wounds were typically smaller than exit wounds in firearm cases. She also said that gunshot residue, commonly found on the hands in suspected suicides, was not tested for in this case.

'Enough is enough': Jamaat-i-Islami announces 510 nationwide sit-ins against the petroleum levy. LAHORE: Jamaat-i-Islami Pakistan (JI) Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Thursday announced peaceful sit-ins against the petroleum levy at 510 locations across the country on Friday, warning that the protests would transform into a movement to overthrow the government if authorities attempted to stop them. Addressing a protest rally by the JI Women’s Wing on Wahdat Road in Lahore against rising petroleum prices and inflation, Rehman said major roads linking districts across Pakistan would be blocked from 4pm onwards; however, ambulances would be allowed to pass without interruption. “If obstacles are created or our peaceful protest against the petroleum levy is blocked, this campaign will turn into an anti-government movement,” he said, demanding that the price of petrol be reduced to Rs225 per litre. JI Lahore Emir Advocate Ziauddin Ansari, Women’s Wing President Dr Humaira Tariq, Samiha Raheel Qazi, Samina Saeed and Uzma Imran also addressed the gathering. Rehman urged the government to accept the public’s demands, warning that it would bear full responsibility for any consequences if it failed to respond. He described the petroleum levy as “extortion” rather than a tax, claiming that the government was collecting Rs125 in taxes on every litre of petrol from ordinary citizens while continuing lavish spending on luxury aircraft and expensive official vehicles . “Enough is enough,” he said. The JI chief argued that petroleum prices had been increased by citing global market conditions during regional conflicts but were not reduced after international crude oil prices fell to $74 per barrel. “The government had collected Rs8 trillion through the petroleum levy without investing any of it in upgrading oil refineries or petroleum infrastructure,” he alleged. “The economy can recover if the government abolishes the petroleum levy,” Rehman asserted. The JI chief said the ruling coalition was disconnected from the hardships faced by ordinary Pakistanis, adding that women were struggling to manage household kitchens due to soaring inflation and, in many cases, were being forced to sell their jewellery to support their families. He also criticised unequal access to education, an unresponsive bureaucracy and restrictions on public dissent, arguing that the country’s governance system had become dysfunctional. The JI chief said that the government had become subservient to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), adding it was imposing taxes and approving an anti-people budget while ignoring recommendations to reduce state expenditures. Reiterating that Friday’s demonstrations would remain peaceful, he called on people from Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Azad Jammu and Kashmir to participate in large numbers. “I urged young people to bring their motorcycles onto the roads and join the sit-ins,” he said, adding major highways would be blocked peacefully to pressure the government into withdrawing the petroleum levy.

Israeli settlers attack West Bank Palestinian community, burn homes. Israeli settlers attacked a small Palestinian community in the occupied West Bank, injuring people, destroying homes and smashing their power source, the military and residents said on Thursday, in the latest in a spate of violent confrontations. AFP journalists in remote Khirbet al-Tuba saw buildings blackened by fire and smoke, the interiors of three homes completely burned and graffiti in Hebrew spray-painted on remaining structures. The dozen solar panels the isolated southern community relies on for power had also been smashed to render them unusable. The Israeli military said it “strongly condemned” the raid and that it had responded after “homes being set on fire and Palestinians being attacked in the area by Israeli civilians” late on Wednesday. People check damaged solar panels, which Palestinians say were damaged by Israeli settlers, in Tuba in Masafer Yatta, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on August 6, 2026. — Reuters “Several Palestinians were injured, among them a girl and a woman. Several structures were also burned,” the military said. “The suspects fled before the forces arrived.” Radwan Jundiya, whose house was torched, told AFP that about 40 settlers attacked the hamlet at around 10 pm. “The settlers started throwing stones. We rushed to protect the women, but they got to my wife and daughter and beat them,” he said. “Then they started spraying something and setting the room on fire. The pictures tell the whole story.” Locals said that five people were wounded in the attack, including Jundiya’s wife and daughter, as well as another child. “From the moment the attack began until daybreak, we spent the whole night standing here, putting out the fires and helping the injured,” Ali Awad, another resident whose son was injured, told AFP . Ibrahim Zein, another resident of Khirbet al-Tuba, told AFP that it was the second time settlers attacked the village. “The first time they burned the well, and this time they destroyed these rooms,” Zein said. “Last night they terrified us. I wasn’t even awake. They woke the children, then came straight to the rooms.” Israeli security forces stop a Palestinian motorist for inspection at a checkpoint during an Israeli military raid in the Qalandia refugee camp in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on August 6, 2026. — AFP Violence by Israeli settlers towards Palestinians in the West Bank has persisted for years, but recent months have seen a surge in attacks. Excluding Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, some 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank among some three million Palestinians. Khirbet al-Tuba is a community of about 100 people in the West Bank region of Masafer Yatta, where shepherding communities face frequent settler violence and home demolitions by the military, which has declared parts of the area an army firing zone. The army said it would investigate, but Palestinians and rights groups complain that such investigations rarely lead to prosecutions, and that violent settlers are able to act with impunity — and the army’s support when clashes break out. “When we used to file complaints with the Israeli police over previous attacks, the Israeli army would come and arrest the (Palestinian) residents,” local activist Osama Makhamreh told AFP on Thursday. All Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which has been occupied since 1967, are illegal under international law. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, the most right-wing in Israel’s history, has drastically increased the number of settlements and settlement outposts in the Palestinian territory. Israeli settler charged over killing of Palestinian activist Prosecutors charged an Israeli settler on Thursday in the killing of Palestinian activist Awdah Hathaleen in the occupied West Bank, the first such indictment since the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023, activists say. “Yinon Eliya Levi [33], from Ma’on, has been charged with allegedly firing toward an area where people were present during a confrontation that developed over earthworks on private land, causing the death of the late Awdah Hathaleen,” Israel’s Ministry of Justice said on X. “The Southern District Prosecutor’s Office has filed an indictment against him … on charges of reckless manslaughter, trespassing, and willful property damage.” Hathaleen, an activist who took part in the production of the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land , was killed in July 2025 during a settler attack on his village of Umm al-Khair, in the southern West Bank. Umm al-Khair sits in the region of Masafer Yatta, where Palestinian communities have faced frequent settler violence and home demolitions by the military, which has declared parts of the area an army firing zone. Israeli rights group B’Tselem said the indictment was the first of its kind for the killing of a Palestinian in the West Bank since the start of the war in Gaza in October 2023, which marked the beginning of a surge in violence in the West Bank. “The decision to indict Yinon Levi is the exception that proves the rule,” B’Tselem spokesman Yair Dvir told AFP , accusing Israel of fostering a culture of impunity that “is not a failure of the system – it is a central component”. Hathaleen’s attorney Eitan Peleg told AFP the indictment “is a very important decision. I hope it will be a precedent in future cases of [Israelis] committing crimes against Palestinians in Palestine. “Many Palestinians are killed by settlers, by the army, but this was the first time a full investigation was held and they had no other option but to charge. This was a very clear case,” he added. Palestinian rights group Al-Haq conducted a forensic investigation of Hathaleen’s killing, using footage in which Levi is seen shooting at a crowd of Palestinians in Umm al-Khair the day he was killed. The US and EU placed sanctions on Levi in April 2024 for previous violent attacks on Palestinians.

'Growing pattern of media curbs': HRCP, PFUJ express concern over new rules for foreign press. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) and the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists (PFUJ) have expressed concerns regarding media freedom after the government mandated foreign media personnel to seek permission for travelling to any city outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi for news coverage. “The requirement that journalists obtain state approval to report from large parts of the country sends a chilling message: that critical reporting is unwelcome,” HRCP noted in a statement on Wednesday about the ‘Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026’. Expressing its deep concern, the commission said the rules would “invariably institutionalise bureaucratic control over news gathering and risk deterring independent reporting on matters of public interest” rather than facilitate journalism. “This is the latest in a growing pattern of restrictions on media freedom in Pakistan. From arbitrary curbs on reporting and increasing censorship to legal and administrative barriers, the space for independent journalism has continued to shrink,” the rights body highlighted. It urged the government to withdraw the “restrictive measures and uphold its constitutional and international obligation to protect freedom of expression”. Similarly, PFUJ “strongly condemned” the new rules and termed them as restrictions on press freedom. In a statement issued on Thursday, PFUJ President Afzal Butt and Secretary General Arshad Ansari said the guidelines amount to “attacking the freedom of expression and putting curbs on press freedom”. “The government has not only banned foreign journalists from visiting most of the areas of Pakistan except major cities, but they have also restricted the movement of Pakistani media persons working with international media outlets. They are not allowed to visit these areas on their own either,” it pointed out. “How can foreign correspondents and their Pakistani colleagues perform their professional duties after this notification?” the PFUJ leaders asked. They further asserted that the move would “only bring disrepute to Pakistan and damage its image”. The PFUJ statement noted, “Pakistan is already ranked very low among the countries that have the worst record in press freedom. And the action of the government would add to it.” It demanded that the government immediately “lift this ban” if it believed in democracy and press freedom, arguing that such a move would also impact the employment of Pakistanis working with international media outlets. “Naturally, if Pakistani journalists working with global media outlets are unable to visit different areas, it means they would not be able to perform their professional responsibilities. Consequently, they would lose their jobs,” it contended. The PFUJ leaders were quoted as saying that such actions “are taken in banana republics, not in countries that claim to follow democratic principles”. “If the demands of PFUJ are not accepted, we would be left with no option but to resort to protest and demonstrations,” it warned. In a post on X, Amnesty International also urged “Pakistan’s authorities to end the escalating restrictions on the right to freedom of expression, including press freedom, access to information, and human rights advocacy”. In a letter addressed to the government, Amnesty, HRCP and others called for the withdrawal of the Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026, which they said placed “onerous restrictions on reporting by foreign journalists”. ‘Step backwards’ The BBC has expressed concern over what it called “new restrictions imposed by Pakistani authorities” on the movement of international media personnel in the country, urging the government to reverse the measures. The broadcaster said the restrictions would affect its ability to report independently from across Pakistan, adding that press freedom was under increasing pressure globally and that the move represented “a step backwards” for media freedom in the country. It said its journalists, including locally based staff, needed to be able to travel freely to cover events and report the views of ordinary citizens. According to the new guidelines, all foreign media personnel will now need a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the information ministry to travel to any city except Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi to produce “news content, story, video, film, documentary or social media content” for official use. Additionally, under the new rules, all entities operating in Pakistan to facilitate foreign media “in any capacity” are also required to register with the ministry’s External Publicity (EP) Wing, as are non-journalists living in Pakistan who render services to foreign media. The guidelines also specify that individuals’ press registration can be suspended or withdrawn for “acts against ideology, sovereignty, security or public order of Pakistan”, and if the EP Wing “deems appropriate at any stage”.

Pakistan, 7 other Muslim countries once again condemn Israeli violations in Gaza Strip: FO. Eight Muslim countries, including Pakistan, have once again condemned Israeli violations in the Gaza Strip, terming them violations of international humanitarian law and relevant United Nations resolutions. The Foreign Office (FO) said on Thursday that foreign ministries of Pakistan, Egypt, Turkiye, Indonesia, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, in a joint statement, condemned the continued humanitarian crisis in the region, which they termed “a clear breach of Israel’s obligations under international law”, as well as the plan to end the conflict outlined by United States President Donald Trump in 2025. The ministers expressed “their strongest condemnation and denunciation of the ongoing Israeli violations in the Gaza Strip, particularly the targeting of healthcare facilities and medical infrastructure, attacks on civilian infrastructure and the continued loss of civilian lives”. They said the continued violence undermined efforts to implement the second phase of the plan, especially after Palestinian factions had accepted the agreement. The statement added that Israel’s actions threatened to derail the political process and “reignite the cycle of escalation”. The eight foreign ministers stressed that the protection of civilians, medical facilities, humanitarian and health workers, as well as the immediate delivery of humanitarian aid, were legal obligations that must not be compromised. They added that the ongoing violations could not be viewed in isolation from ongoing settler attacks in the Occupied West Bank, unlawful expansion of settlements, and the “unilateral measures aimed at altering the ‘status quo in Occupied Jerusalem’”, referring to frequent instances of Israeli settlers storming the Al-Aqsa Mosque — one of Islam’s holiest sites. The Israeli government has publicly maintained that its policy on the status quo remains unchanged, even as incidents like last Thursday’s continue to inflame the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. However, since taking office, its far-right Security Minister Ben Gvir has stormed Al-Aqsa Mosque more than a dozen times. “Taken together, these practices constitute a systematic policy aimed at imposing a fait accompli by force, undermining the foundations of the two-state solution, and marginalising the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people,” the statement said. Reiterating that these actions violated international humanitarian law and relevant United Nations resolutions, the ministers once again called on the international community — particularly the UN Security Council — to compel Israel to fulfill its obligations under those laws while holding to account “those responsible for grave violations”. They added that this should be done in a way that contributes to civilian protection and achieving a permanent ceasefire. They rejected attempts to annex or impose Israeli sovereignty over the occupied territory or to forcibly displace Palestinians, stressing that a “serious political process” leading to a two-state solution was the only path to a just and comprehensive peace. This process, they added, should include the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state based on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. At a ministerial conference in Amman, Jordan on Wednesday, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said that Israel has no sovereignty over East Jerusalem and its holy sites, condemning the incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque by “extremist Israeli settlers”. On the sidelines of the meeting, Dar also held one-on-one meetings with the foreign ministers of Turkiye, Algeria and Egypt, as well as his Jordanian counterpart, with the “deteriorating situation in the occupied West Bank” coming under discussion.

Daily flights to Riyadh from 14th. KARACHI: Saudi Arabia’s new national carrier, Riyadh Air, has announced an expansion of its routes to Pakistan, with daily flights connecting the two capitals set to commence on August 14. In a statement, the airline said that ticket sales had started for the Islamabad-Riyadh and Lahore-Riyadh routes, while the inaugural service to Lahore would be launched on August 18. A total of seven flights per week would operate between Riyadh and Islamabad, while the Lahore route would be served by three flights per week, the statement said. The airline said that the new routes will be operated on Riyadh Air’s new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, featuring the airline’s latest cabin interiors and on-board experience. The Dreamliners feature four cabins, including Business Elite, Business, Premium Economy and Economy class. The Lahore-Riyadh and Islamabad-Riyadh routes have been planned to offer smooth onward connectivity to Europe and the Middle East, catering to both business and leisure travellers from Pakistan, the statement said. Published in Dawn, August 7th, 2026

Hormuz shipping prospects remain uncertain. • Tanker reports fresh explosions in strait; US naval blockade remains in place • US imports of Middle East crude set to cross 0.6m barrels per day • Vance, Ghalibaf trade barbs over ‘messy negotiations’ WASHINGTON / TEH­RAN: Despite an understanding between Iran and Oman, fresh security incidents in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday highlighted the continued risks for regional shipping in the critical waterway. While the agreement would be a step towards reopening the key energy route, Iranian media stressed that any easing still hinged on Washington ending its own naval blockade of Iran’s ports. On Thursday, Centcom said it continued to enforce the naval blockade of Iran, redirecting 49 commercial vessels, disabling two, and boarding two. Highlighting the risks to ships, the captain of an oil tanker reported hearing two explosions while transiting the strait, nine nautical miles southeast of Kumzar in Oman, Britain’s maritime security agency said on Wednesday. “The Master of a tanker has reported hearing two explosions whilst transiting in the Strait of Hormuz,” the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on X, adding that the crew and vessel were safe, and that no environmental damage was reported. Oman is already facing an impending environmental catastrophe as an alleged Russian shadow fleet tanker leaks oil across hundreds of square kilometres near a nature reserve. Satellite imagery shows what appeared to be an oil slick spreading from a ship that has been stranded for over a month near al-Qibliyyah island, off Oman’s southern coast. It is far from the Strait of Hormuz, which has seen regular tanker attacks in the Middle East war. “With oil apparently continuing to leak and the vessel stranded in a difficult location, the risk of an even larger environmental disaster remains serious,” Nina Noelle of Greenpeace told AFP. She warned of a “severe and long-lasting” consequence. US imports cross 0.6m barrels per day US imports of Middle Eastern crude are set to hit about 600,000 barrels per day in August, the highest since the Iran war began, as a brief opening of the Strait of Hormuz and the rerouting of Saudi oil through the Suez Canal pushed barrels toward American ports, ship-tracking data showed. Nearly a dozen ships loaded with Middle Eastern crude were headed to US ports as American refiners and traders moved swiftly to snap up barrels that exited the strait when a memorandum of understanding signed by US and Iran in June helped release vessels from the maritime choke point. Also boosting imports are cargoes from Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea port of Yanbu that are traveling through the Suez Canal to the United States. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude output to Yanbu via its east-west pipeline to get around Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. However, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militants last month launched a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, and the risk of attacks at the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on the southern end of the Red Sea has forced many tankers to head north and exit the shipping channel via the Suez Canal. That has increased exports from the region to the United States, as the journey to US ports from the Suez Canal is shorter than the route to Asia. Vessels exiting via the northern route can still sail to Asia, but the voyage would take nearly four weeks longer than typical and raise costs. ‘Theatre’ of negotiations Meanwhile, US Vice President JD Vance acknowledged American frustrations with the pace of diplomacy with Iran, saying negotiations would take time because of divisions within the country’s leadership. “It’s going to be messy and it’s going to take some time to get there,” Vance told Fox News in an interview broadcast on Wednesday. “The reality… is that number one, the Iranians are extraordinarily difficult people. Number two, they have a fractured system,” he said. On the other hand, Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf assailed the US for using “bullying, broken promises [and] fake news as leverage” during negotiations. “‘Massive attack coming … wait, never mind, they want to negotiate,’” he writes on X, in an apparent jibe at Washington’s attitude throughout the peace process. “That’s theatre diplomacy on loop.” Calling the US approach a “failed strategy”, he urges Washington to acknowledge facts and fulfil its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding. “We don’t need more theatre,” he concluded. Published in Dawn, August 7th, 2026

Govt mulls bypassing Zardari’s assent for judges’ appointment. • President has yet to approve summary for JCP-recommended hirings • Govt reviewing possibility of issuing notifications under Article 48(1) • Presidency sources warn bypassing procedure may lead to complications • IHC reserves verdict on maintainability of plea challenging delay in notifying appointments ISLAMABAD: The federal government is considering notifying the appointment and confirmation of high court judges despite President Asif Ali Zardari not having formally accorded assent to the recommendations made by the Judicial Commission of Pakis­tan (JCP), sources told Dawn. The JCP, during its meetings held on July 20 and 21, recommended the appointment of 19 additional judges to the high courts, confirmed the services of four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court and one additional judge of the Lahore High Court, and extended the tenure of an additional judge of the Sindh High Court by six months. However, the appointments have yet to be notified by the Ministry of Law and Justice as the president has not formally approved the summary. According to informed sources, the government is examining the possibility of invoking Article 48(1) of the Constitution to issue the notification, arguing that the president was required to act on the summary within a fortnight of its submission. Since that period has expired, they believe the government may proceed with the appointments. The sources said the delay had already created practical complications. Four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court, whose services were confirmed by the JCP, ceased to hold office after the exp­iry of their tenure on Aug 4 due to the absence of a formal notification. Similarly, an additional judge of the Sindh High Court, whose tenure had been extended by the JCP for another six months, also relinquished office after his term expired on July 29. When contacted, Minister of State for Law and Justice Barrister Aqeel Malik said the government would resolve the matter within the constitutional framework and in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Constitution and the principles laid down by the superior courts. However, sources in the Presidency cautioned against bypassing the prescribed procedure, warning that any such move could trigger political and legal complications. They said Articles 48(1) and 48(2), which define the respective constitutional roles of the president and the prime minister, as well as Article 175A(8), which deals with the appointment of judges, left room for differing interpretations. According to Presidency sou­rces, any ambiguity should be resolved through mutual consultation between the president and the prime minister rather than through unilateral action. On the other hand, government sources maintained that judicial appointments were governed by constitutional provisions and that any deadlock must be resolved strictly in accordance with the Constitution. IHC reserves verdict on plea The Islamabad High Court reserved its verdict on the maintainability of a plea challenging President Zardari’s delay in approving a summary for the appointment and confirmation of judges to various high courts. The writ petition, filed by advocate Luqman Zafar Chaudhary through his counsel Zahid Asif Chaudhry, urged the court to direct the president to approve the summary forwarded by the prime minister for the judicial appointments recommended by the JCP. Justice Arbab Muhammad Tahir took up the plea on Thursday, with the petitioner’s counsel arguing that the JCP had recommended the appointments during its meetings on July 20 and 21. He contended that the summary had reportedly not been approved by the president even after 15 days had passed. The petitioner’s counsel told the court that reports suggested the government might issue notifications for the appointments in the next 48 hours. During the hearing, the contents of his client’s plea were also read out on the court’s direction, and Justice Tahir repeatedly questioned whether a constitutional petition could be maintained against the president. He asked the counsel to cite any precedent in which a writ had been issued against the president. The court also observed that the judgements cited by the petitioner did not support the proposition advanced by his counsel for issuing directives to the president. The court asked the lawyer to identify any decision in which a court had issued directions to the president regarding the exercise of powers under Article 48 of the Constitution. Article 48 states that the president shall act “on and in accordance with the advice of the cabinet or the prime minister”. However, it adds that the president can ask the cabinet or the PM to reconsider the advice within 15 days of receiving it and shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration within 10 days. Sources in the Presidency have contended that the provision also empowered the president and did not set a timeframe for appointments. They cited its second clause, which states: “The president shall act in his discretion in respect of any matter in respect of which he is empowered by the Constitution to do so.” However, legal experts have noted that the SC had previously held that the president lacked discretion in appointing superior court judges and must follow the PM’s advice. The petitioner’s lawyer argued that notifications for judicial appointments were usually issued by the law ministry after the president’s approval, but the ministry could issue them even without presidential assent. He contended that the president’s role in the process was ceremonial and that if approval was withheld, the competent authority should proceed with issuing the notification. After hearing his arguments, the court dec­lined the request to issue notices at this stage and rese­rved its decision on the maintainability of the petition. Published in Dawn, August 7th, 2026

The Petroleum Division’s notification said the new prices would be applicable for August 7 (Friday). The diesel price has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Pakistan to emulate Chinese techniques of investigation. • Naqvi says centre in Islamabad will combine detention, investigation and summary trial facilities under one roof • Initiative aims to speed up disposal of minor offence cases, reduce procedural delays ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is set to embark on a major transformation of its policing system, with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi announcing a series of reforms inspired by successful international law enforcement models, including the establishment of a China-style Law Enforcement Investigation Centre in Islamabad. The announcement came during his meeting with assistant superintendents of police who recently returned after completing specialised training courses in China and Turkiye. The officers described overseas programmes as an invaluable experience that significantly enhanced their professional capabilities and exposed them to modern policing practices, surveillance technologies, and contemporary approaches to maintaining law and order. Acknowledging the importance of international exposure, Naqvi declared that foreign training programmes would become a permanent component of the professional development of Pakistani police officers. He emphasised that the government was committed to equipping the country’s law enforcement agencies with the skills and technologies required to address emerging security challenges. As part of the reforms, the interior minister announced the launch of a pilot project to establish a China-style Law Enforcement Investigation Centre in Islamabad. The centre will integrate detention, investigation and summary trial facilities under one roof, enabling the swift and efficient disposal of cases involving minor offences while reducing procedural delays. Naqvi said the country would benefit from internationally proven policing models to make its law-enforcement system more effective, responsive, and technology-driven. He stressed that the adoption of advanced surveillance systems and modern technologies would significantly expand monitoring capabilities and strengthen crime prevention efforts. To further enhance public safety, the interior minister announced that modern drones would be inducted into the Aviation Wing of the Ministry of Interior to improve surveillance and support law enforcement operations. The reform agenda also includes strengthening investigative capacity through the establishment of specialised investigation rooms at the National Police Academy. According to the interior minister, greater emphasis will be placed on specialised investigation training aligned with the evolving requirements of modern policing. He further announced that interrogations would be introduced as a specialised academic subject within police training, with modern interrogation techniques based on the practices of developed countries becoming an integral part of the curriculum. In another key initiative, Naqvi revealed plans to introduce new police uniforms designed to better meet the operational requirements of law-enforcement personnel, reflecting the practical demands of contemporary policing. During the meeting, the ASPs shared their observations on advanced policing systems in China and Turkiye, highlighting the effective use of surveillance technologies, modern equipment, digital tools, and public security management practices that could be adapted to Pakistan’s policing framework. The Commandant of the National Police Academy, the Director General of the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), and other senior officials also attended the meeting. Ex-Afghan general, agent’s pleas against arrest, deportation rejected. • Petitioners cite fear of Taliban persecution if sent back to Afghanistan • Peshawar High Court notes fears of detention and removal don’t constitute valid cause of action • Rules immigration, visa and residency matters fall within executive’s domain PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court (PHC) has rejected petitions filed by a former general of the erstwhile Afghan National Army and a special agent of the former Afghan Presidential Protective Service (PPS), along with their families, seeking protection against their imminent arrest and deportation by law enforcement agencies. A bench comprising Justices Wiqar Ahmad and Kamran Hayat Miankhel dismissed two almost identical petitions filed by former general Baryalai Sharifi and former PPS special agent Abdul Mujeeb Ghairat and their family members. They had approached the court fearing persecution by the Taliban government in Afghanistan if deported. The counsel for Mr Sharifi submitted that his clients were Afghan nationals who had entered Pakistan on valid visas. He claimed that Mr Sharifi had served as a general in the former Afghan National Army (Milli Urdu) and that he and his family had received threats from the present Afghan regime. He added that Mr Sharifi’s wife had served as an assistant doctor in the PPS of the former Afghan government, while his son claimed to have worked as a training camp guard in the same service. The counsel further stated that Mr Sharifi had approached the Society for Human Rights and Prisoners’ Aid (SHARP) for pre-screening in connection with an international protection and resettlement process, and apprehended that the petitioners might be arrested or deported from Pakistan. ‘Mere apprehension’ “The petitioners have not challenged any specific order, notification or action of the respondents adversely affecting their legal or fundamental rights,” the bench observed in its four-page written order. “The entire case rests upon a mere apprehension that they may, in future, be subjected to arrest, detention or deportation. Such speculative apprehension, without any concrete cause of action or demonstrated violation of law, does not furnish a valid ground for invoking the extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction of this court under Article 199 of the Constitution,” it added. The court observed that “matters relating to the stay of foreign nationals in Pakistan, grant, extension or cancellation of visas, and their immigration status are governed by the relevant statutory framework and fall within the exclusive domain of the competent executive authorities”. “Any request for international protection, refugee processing or resettlement through SHARP, UNHCR or any third country does not, by itself, create an enforceable legal right against the respondents capable of being enforced through a constitutional petition,” it held. Similarly, in the case of Mr Ghairat, counsel submitted that the petitioner and his family were residing in Pakistan on valid visas and had applied online for their renewal. He stated that Mr Ghairat had served as a special agent in the former PPS, an elite US-trained security unit responsible for the close protection of the then Afghan president. The counsel argued that owing to his previous service under the former Afghan government, Mr Ghairat and his family would face danger if returned to Afghanistan. He contended that in view of the ongoing action against certain Afghan nationals, the petitioners feared arrest and deportation despite their claimed lawful stay in Pakistan. “The questions relating to the petitioners’ right to remain in Pakistan, renewal or extension of visas, or their immigration status fall within the exclusive domain of the competent executive authorities under the relevant immigration and foreigner laws,” the bench observed. “In the absence of any unlawful action, refusal of a statutory request, or infringement of a vested legal right, no writ can be issued directing the respondents to grant protection or confer a legal status upon the petitioners.” Published in Dawn, August 7th, 2026

Terrorist havens. DESPITE the use of both carrots and sticks by the international community, the Afghan Taliban refuse to cut their ties to terrorist groups such as the TTP. This poses a particular problem to Afghanistan’s neighbours, including Pakistan, which has borne the brunt of terrorist violence ever since the Taliban’s return to Kabul in 2021 . Both KP and Balochistan are currently in the grip of violent insurgencies, with the elements responsible for the bloodshed finding safe havens in Afghanistan. Pakistan raised the issue at the UN Security Council on Wednesday, with this country’s permanent representative highlighting the “increasingly permissive environment” for terrorist groups in Afghanistan after the Taliban takeover. He urged the Taliban to fulfil their obligations and ensure Afghan soil is not used against neighbouring states. China’s representative at the same forum echoed these concerns, urging the Taliban to take action, whilst supporting Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts. The Chinese diplomat also called for sanctions on the BLA and Majeed Brigade. These issues have been raised repeatedly, while UNSC monitoring reports have endorsed Pakistan’s concerns regarding the permissive environment for terrorist groups in Afghanistan. It is not just the TTP; Al Qaeda, IS-K, ETIM and others are all believed to be active in Afghanistan. While the Taliban are opposed to IS-K, they have deep links with other violent actors. Moreover, nearly all of Afghanistan’s neighbours have complained of the threat these outfits pose to their security. Yet the Taliban only pay lip service to these concerns, denying the fact that terrorists operate from their territory. These denials are implausible as there is a convincing body of evidence proving that violent outfits operate in an agreeable atmosphere in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan. As this paper has argued before, a regional response is required to tackle the problem of Afghanistan-based terrorist groups. The Afghan Taliban are an unpalatable reality and cannot be wished away. The challenge for the international community is to use a combination of deterrence and incentives to make them change their tune. Pakistan has tried kinetic methods to deter cross-border terrorism, but in the long term, continued hostilities are not sustainable. The economic situation in Afghanistan is dire, and its people live in misery. Instead of protecting their terrorist comrades, the Taliban need to think about improving the lives of common Afghans. This can only happen through trade and regional integration. Yet Afghanistan will remain a pariah if its rulers keep harbouring terrorists. Therefore, Kabul’s neighbours need to continue diplomatic, political and, where needed, kinetic efforts to end the ‘export’ of terrorism from Afghanistan, both for its own development, and regional peace.
